quote: (a) Kubient agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer and its officers, directors, managers, members, agents, and employees from all third-party allegations, claims, actions, losses, expenses, damages, costs (including, without limitation, reasonable attorneys' fees) or liabilities ("Claims") arising out of or in connection with:
rationale: Section 10(a) gives us an express Vendor duty to defend, indemnify and hold harmless AP against all third-party Claims arising out of the Services, the Auction Platform, Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty, and the acts or omissions of Kubient and its subcontractors. Read with the §9(b) warranties — non-infringement of the Service and deliverables (9(b)(i)), data security (9(b)(iii)), and compliance with applicable Laws (9(b)(v), (ix)) — the indemnity captures third-party IP infringement, Vendor-caused data breach, Vendor breach of law, and Vendor negligence/misconduct. Section 11 supplies the standard procedure: prompt written notice (with no forfeiture for delay), indemnitor control of defence and settlement subject to our consent to any liability admission, and reasonable cooperation at the indemnifying party's cost. This exceeds the fallback: the IP indemnity carries none of the permitted Customer modification/combination/specification exclusions, and there is no 3x annual fees super-cap anywhere in the Agreement — indeed §7(a) carves indemnification liability out of the consequential-damages waiver, so Kubient's exposure is uncapped in our favour. The fallback procure/modify/replace/refund remedy ladder is absent, but that ladder and the super-cap are Vendor-side protections whose omission benefits us and does not weaken our recovery. Two points fall short of preferred wording only and are noted rather than redlined: affiliates are not named among the indemnitees (officers, directors, managers, members, agents and employees are), and our §10(b) indemnity is broader than "Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law" — it also covers unauthorised use of the Services/Platform, breach of our warranties, and our acts or omissions. The fallback checklist contains no Customer-indemnity element, so the bargain is met on its material terms and we would not reopen a favourable, uncapped Vendor indemnity to chase that wording.

rationale: Section 7 is the only liability provision in the Agreement (searches for cap, aggregate and exceed language return nothing else; Sections 10-11 indemnities and Section 13 disclaimer contain no cap). It provides a mutual exclusion of consequential, incidental, indirect, punitive and special damages, with carve-outs for indemnification and breach of confidentiality, but it contains no aggregate liability cap of any kind. The fallback therefore fails on its central material term: there is no mutual cap and no 12-months-of-fees basis, leaving our direct liability unlimited. We inserted a single Section 7(b) sentence establishing a mutual cap of the fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim, with indemnification, confidentiality, gross negligence and willful misconduct expressly outside the cap. We used "fees paid or payable under this Agreement" rather than "by Customer" because Section 5 operates as a revenue share, so a Customer-paid-fees basis would be illusory. The preferred USD 1,000,000 floor and the additional preferred carve-outs (data protection/security, fraud, IP infringement, payment obligations) are not pursued at this fallback target.

verification.notes: All four fallback elements are met in operative language: the new 9(b)(xii) supplies the missing 90-day express software-to-documentation warranty, the new sentence supplies the previously absent repair/replace/refund remedy, and the retained ongoing Service warranties in 9(b)(ii) and (vi) exceed the 30-day services floor. The finding is correctly classified as a deviation cured at fallback. Preferred is not reached: no "professional and workmanlike manner" services standard and only a 90-day (not 12-month) software conformance period; the no-malicious-code limb cannot be confirmed from the supplied text. These are noted as short of preferred, consistent with the drafter's own framing. Minimality holds: the edit is a single concise insertion at the end of Kubient's existing warranty list, deletes nothing (including the Customer-favourable disclaimer carve-out "except for the representations and warranties set forth in this Agreement"), and adds no survival tail, expense allocation, notice procedure or damages category outside the checklist. Electing "at Customer's election" rather than Vendor's option is a permissible Customer-side formulation of the same remedy element and adds no new requirement. Intent is preserved: paragraph 13's express-warranty carve-out means the new warranty is not swallowed by the AS IS disclaimer; no cross-reference is broken and no retained sentence contradicts the insertion. "documentation provided by Kubient" is lower-case descriptive language, not an undefined capitalised term, so it creates no dangling definition. Two watch-items for the drafter, neither fatal: (1) confirm "Auction Platform" is a defined term elsewhere in the Agreement, otherwise substitute "the Service" to avoid a dangling reference; (2) the remedy sentence is drafted to cover breach of all warranties "in this paragraph 9(b)" — this is broader than the two remedy elements strictly require, though it is Customer-favourable and does not import any new obligation, so it does not defeat minimality. If Vendor pushes back, narrowing it to the conformance and Service performance warranties is the cleanest retreat.

verification.notes: The Agreement contains no insurance covenant anywhere (confirmed by the cited General Provisions in Section 14 and the deterministic 'insurance obligation present' check now keying only on the inserted text), so a concise insertion is the correct remedy for a 'missing' finding. Fallback is complete: both atomic elements (E&O ≥ USD 1,000,000; cyber ≥ USD 2,000,000) appear in a single operative sentence imposing a maintenance obligation on Kubient, the Vendor. Preferred is incomplete on four counts — no CGL per-occurrence or aggregate limits, E&O at 1M rather than 2M, cyber at 2M rather than 5M, no workers' compensation, and no certificates-on-request. These are not defects to repair given the fallback level was deliberately selected for this low-severity rule. Minimality holds: the drafter omitted the model-language extras (at-own-expense, throughout-the-term-plus-one-year survival tail, certificates) that are not required by the chosen fallback checklist, deleted no existing words, and added nothing outside the two selected elements. Intent is preserved: the insertion is appended as a free-standing covenant after Section 14(i), creates no dangling cross-reference or undefined term, and does not contradict the security obligations in 9(b)(iii) or any other allocation.
